 Kentucky company paid $800,000 for Ohio river land, but why was its compensation lawsuit over floodplain rules ruled premature
 SECTIONS Kentucky company paid $800,000 for Ohio river land, but why was its compensation lawsuit over floodplain rules ruled premature By Shreya Biswas , Global Desk Last Updated: Nov 05, 2026, 07:36:00 PM IST Rate Story Follow us Share Font Size Abc Small Abc Medium Abc Large Save Print Comment Synopsis A Kentucky company that bought four acres along the Ohio River for $800,000 sued local authorities, claiming floodplain rules had stripped the property of its economic value. But an appeals court rejected the claim, saying the company had never applied for a variance or obtained a final decision on what it could build.
 Kentucky company paid $800,000 for Ohio river land, but why was its compensation lawsuit over floodplain rules ruled premature (Photo: AI/Gemini)
 A Kentucky company bought four acre property along the Ohio River for $800000 in 1998. Then more than two decades later, it went to court, arguing that floodplain regulations had stripped the land of its economic value. However, the judges said the company had filed its claim too soon cause it never applied for an exception to the restrictions or obtained a final decision on what could be built there.
 Lampton Securities Partnership had purchased the property after local floodplain ordinances were introduced in 1997. The regulations restricted most new construction in the area, but they also allowed property owners to seek permission for exceptions.
Lampton never applied for one. Instead it sued Louisville-Jefferson County Metro Government and the Metropolitan Sewer District, seeking compensation on the grounds that the restrictions had taken away all economically beneficial uses of the land, as per a Justia report. 
The Kentucky Court of Appeals rejected the company's claim on October 30 2026, and also upheld a lower court's decision in favor of the two government agencies. The judges said there had been no final decision on what Lampton could build on the property, making its compensation lawsuit premature.
 Kentucky Company Bought Ohio River Land After Floodplain Rules Took Effect
The property covers roughly four acres along the Ohio River. In the early 1990s, its previous owners received approval from the Metropolitan Sewer District for a condominium project divided into two phases.

 The first phase was completed on about two acres. The remaining two acres were intended for the second phase, where the owners also installed an electrical equipment building and utility lines. However, no condominiums were built on that portion.
 In 1997, Louisville-Jefferson County Metro Government introduced floodplain ordinances following catastrophic flooding. The rules restricted most new construction in the floodplain's conveyance zone, where the remaining property was located.
 The regulations included exceptions. Construction that had already begun before the rules took effect could continue, while affected property owners could also apply to the Metropolitan Sewer District's Floodplain Board for a variance.
Lampton purchased the remaining tract in 1998 for $800,000 after the restrictions were already in place. The property remained unused until the company put it on market around 2019. Its marketing materials described the land as suitable for commercial development.

 Kentucky Ohio River land lawsuit (Photo: AI/Gemini)
 Company Sued Government After Being Told Development Was Not Allowed
The dispute gained momentum when Metropolitan Sewer District personnel learned that the property was being marketed for sale. A meeting followed between the agency's counsel and Lampton, during which the counsel said the floodplain ordinances prevented development on the land.
Lampton did not apply to the Floodplain Board for a variance. It also did not try to begin the second phase of the previously approved condominium project and wait for local authorities to respond.
Instead, the company filed a reverse condemnation lawsuit against Metro Government and the sewer district in May 2020. It argued that the floodplain restrictions had taken away all economically beneficial uses of the property.

 Jefferson Circuit Court judge had granted summary judgment to the government agencies in July 2025. And then Lampton challenged that decision and took the case to the Kentucky Court of Appeals.
 Judges Said Lampton Had Not Exhausted Its Options
In its October 30 ruling, the Kentucky Court of Appeals focused on whether Lampton had received a final decision from the authorities about what could be built on the property.
The judges said the opinion given by the sewer district's counsel was not a final decision. The authority to grant exceptions rested with the Floodplain Board, not the agency's staff.
The court also pointed to evidence that the board had granted variances to other property owners. Since Lampton had never submitted an application, there was no way to know whether its request would have been approved or rejected.
The company argued that applying for a variance would have been pointless. The judges disagreed, saying Lampton had not shown that the board would certainly reject its request or that seeking an exception would have been futile.
The court also noted that Lampton had never tried to begin construction under the earlier condominium approval and then been stopped by local authorities.
Without a final decision on the property's permitted uses, the judges said they couldn't determine whether the floodplain regulations had actually taken away all economically beneficial use of the land.
 Court Leaves Open the Possibility of Future Compensation Claim
Appeals court upheld the summary judgment in favor of Louisville-Jefferson County Metro Government and the Metropolitan Sewer District.
However, the decision did not permanently rule out compensation for Lampton. The judges noted that the company could bring another takings claim in the future if it became legally ripe and met the other requirements for such a case.
The court made no ruling on how a future claim would be decided or what defenses the government agencies might raise.
The ruling means Lampton lost its current lawsuit because it had not obtained a final decision on what it could do with the property before seeking compensation.
